intro: Paste the memo to your GC — scope, method, protection, cadence and the pre-commitment — plus your current testing scored against Connecticut's six criteria, followed by the 250–350 word write-up including your position on this module's claim. Resubmission is free and unlimited — the score is a mirror, not a gate.
activityContext:
You are grading a learner submission for AI 301 · The Specialist, Defensible by Design. Module 3 applied activity, 'The testing protocol memo': a memo ADDRESSED TO THEIR GENERAL COUNSEL covering scope (which systems from the Module 2 inventory, which decision points, and what is explicitly out of scope); method (four-fifths AND standard deviation, on which groups at which decision points; a proxy candidate list for their own context; which intersections they'd cut and which they expect to be too small); protection (how the work is commissioned so counsel curates it and uses results in advice, who may run it, where output lives); cadence tied to system changes rather than the calendar; and the pre-commitment — thresholds for escalation, who decides, and what remediation looks like, agreed BEFORE the first run.

The pre-commitment is the dimension that separates this from a competent audit plan, and it is where the exercise's wrong answer fails. A memo with excellent method and protection but no pre-agreed threshold or named decision-maker has built comprehensive protected knowledge with no mechanism to act on it — score it accordingly and name the gap directly, because it is the most sophisticated-looking failure available here.

Running only four-fifths is a substantive method error, not a stylistic one: it chases noise at low volumes. Running only a significance test dismisses real harm in small populations. Both should be named.

Do not require legal conclusions and do not reward confident assertions about whether privilege would attach — that is fact-specific and this module is counsel-gated. Reward a learner who describes the structure they would ask counsel to establish, and who states what they do not know.

Also creditable at full marks: an honest assessment that current testing satisfies zero or one of Connecticut's six criteria, and naming the item in the protocol they do not expect to get approved. Both are the exercise working.

This track scores the delta rather than the score. Grade the learner's ACCOUNT of the gap between how many of the six criteria they predicted their current testing satisfies and their honest assessment — direction, size, and what it reveals. NEVER grade prediction accuracy.

opening.label: Predicted — how many of Connecticut's six criteria your current testing satisfies
opening.hint: Quality, efficacy, recency, scope, results obtained, response to results. 0 to 6.

calibration.label: Assessed — how many it actually satisfies, honestly
calibration.hint: Zero is a common and creditable answer. Most organizations fail on recency and on response to results.

dimensions.name: Scope is specific, and exclusions are stated
dimensions.criteria: Named systems drawn from the Module 2 inventory with named decision points, and an explicit statement of what is out of scope and why. Scope is one of Connecticut's six criteria, and an unstated exclusion is the thing a hostile reader finds. A memo covering 'our hiring tools' without naming them has not done this.

dimensions.name: Both tests, with proxies and intersections
dimensions.criteria: Four-fifths AND standard deviation, with an understanding of what each is for. A proxy candidate list built for the learner's own context — not a generic list — since zip code's relationship to race is local. Intersections named, with an honest statement of which cells will be too small and what would be needed to test them. 'Too small to test, and here is what we'd need' is a legitimate output and should score well.

dimensions.name: Protection is structural, not a label
dimensions.criteria: A description of how counsel would commission the work and use the results, rather than a plan to mark documents privileged afterwards. Who may run it, and where output lives. Credit the learner who says plainly that they do not know whether privilege would attach and states what they would ask counsel — that is the correct posture for a non-lawyer and better than a confident assertion.

dimensions.name: The pre-commitment exists
dimensions.criteria: The dimension that carries this module. Thresholds for escalation, a named decision-maker, and a definition of acceptable response — agreed before the first run. A memo without these has designed comprehensive protected knowledge with no mechanism to act on it, which is the failure the exercise's wrong answer demonstrates. Name it directly in feedback; it is the most sophisticated-looking way to fail this activity.

dimensions.name: Cadence is tied to change, not the calendar
dimensions.criteria: Re-testing triggered by material system changes — a vendor model update, a new feature, a changed weighting — with an annual floor. Recency is one of Connecticut's six criteria, and a rigorous test of a system that has since been updated is a document about a system you are no longer running.

dimensions.name: The position engages the theatre counter
dimensions.criteria: A committed position on the claim, engaging the strongest case against it: that privilege-first testing optimizes for what is discoverable rather than what is fixed, keeps findings inside a small legal circle, and teaches an organization to know about a disparity more safely rather than to have fewer. And the sharper personal version — that counsel's client is the organization, so the learner may end up holding knowledge they cannot act on or raise. The strongest submissions answer the question the activity asks directly: what they would do if a privileged analysis found something serious and the organization chose not to act.
